usage: 저는 강남에 있는 회사에서 근무해요.
I work at a company in Gangnam.
근무하다 = where/how you are employed; more formal than 일하다, common on documents and intros.
주 5일 근무합니다.
I work a 5-day week.
Set phrases like 주 5일 근무 / 재택 근무 / 야간 근무 use 근무 a lot — learn them as chunks.
examples: 몇 시부터 근무하세요?
What time do you start work?
Asking a coworker's hours; 근무하다 sounds more professional than 일하다 here.
다음 달부터 다른 지점에서 근무하게 됐어요.
Starting next month I'll be working at a different branch.
-게 됐어요 shows it was decided by circumstance, not your own choice.
저희 팀은 보통 9시부터 6시까지 근무해요.
Our team usually works from 9 to 6.
저희 = humble 'our', natural when talking about your own company.
nuance: 근무하다 is the workplace word for 'to work / be on duty', focused on your employment or shift rather than the physical act of doing tasks. Koreans use it constantly in fixed phrases: 재택근무 (working from home), 야간근무 (night shift), 주 5일 근무 (5-day week). In casual chat with friends 일하다 is more common, but at the office, on contracts, and in self-introductions 근무하다 sounds natural and polished.
mistakes: Don't say 근무해요 for a one-off task like cleaning your desk — 근무하다 is about being employed/on shift, not doing a specific chore (use 하다 or 일하다).

usage: 제가 이 프로젝트를 담당하고 있어요.
I'm in charge of this project.
Use 을/를 담당하다 — the thing you're responsible for takes the object particle.
마케팅을 담당하는 김 대리예요.
This is Assistant Manager Kim, who handles marketing.
담당하는 + person introduces 'the person responsible for ~' — very common when introducing colleagues.
examples: 이 건은 누가 담당하세요?
Who is in charge of this matter?
이 건 = 'this case/matter', standard office wording for a task or issue.
저는 해외 거래처를 담당하고 있습니다.
I'm in charge of our overseas clients.
-고 있습니다 = formal ongoing; good for emails and meetings.
담당자가 지금 자리에 안 계셔서요.
The person in charge isn't at their desk right now.
담당자 (the noun 'person in charge') is everywhere in offices and customer service.
nuance: 담당하다 means to officially be responsible for a specific task, client, or area at work. The derived noun 담당자 ('the person in charge') is one of the most-used office words — you'll hear 담당자분께 전달할게요 (I'll pass it to the person in charge) constantly. It implies an assigned, ongoing duty, so it's stronger and more formal than just 하다. Use it to clarify roles, route requests, and introduce who owns what.
mistakes: The thing you handle is the object: 마케팅을 담당해요, not 마케팅에 담당해요.

usage: 이번 발표는 제가 맡을게요.
I'll take on this presentation.
맡다 = to take on a role/task yourself; warmer and more proactive than the formal 담당하다.
새로운 업무를 맡게 됐어요.
I've been given a new job/duty.
-게 됐어요 frames it as assigned to you; 업무 = work duties.
examples: 그 일은 제가 맡겠습니다.
I'll take that on.
맡겠습니다 = formal 'I will take it'; sounds reliable and willing in a meeting.
부장님이 저한테 그 프로젝트를 맡기셨어요.
The department head assigned me that project.
맡기다 (to entrust/hand over) is the causative pair of 맡다 — note the 기.
제가 이 부분 맡을 테니까 너무 걱정하지 마세요.
I'll handle this part, so don't worry too much.
-(으)ㄹ 테니까 = 'I will ~, so'; reassuring tone with a coworker.
nuance: 맡다 is the everyday verb for taking on a role or responsibility — a task, a project, a part of the work. It feels more personal and active than 담당하다 (which is the official 'assigned to'), so volunteering with 제가 맡을게요 sounds proactive and team-friendly. Watch the spelling: the stem ends in ㅌ, giving 맡아요 / 맡았어요 (NOT a ㄷ-irregular). Its causative partner 맡기다 means to entrust the task to someone else.
mistakes: Not a ㄷ-irregular: it's 맡아요/맡았어요, never 마라요. Also don't confuse 맡다 (take charge) with 맡기다 (entrust to someone).

usage: 결과를 팀장님께 보고했어요.
I reported the results to the team leader.
Report TO a person uses 께/에게(한테); the content takes 을/를.
이 내용 부장님께 보고드릴게요.
I'll report this to the manager.
보고드리다 = humble form of 보고하다, used when reporting up to a superior.
examples: 진행 상황을 매주 보고해야 해요.
I have to report the progress every week.
진행 상황 = 'progress/status', a core office phrase.
문제가 생기면 바로 보고해 주세요.
If a problem comes up, please report it right away.
바로 = immediately; common instruction from a manager.
방금 일어난 일을 그대로 보고했습니다.
I reported exactly what just happened.
그대로 = 'as it is, exactly'; useful for factual reporting.
nuance: 보고하다 is the formal verb for reporting information up a hierarchy — to a boss, a client, or headquarters. In Korea's hierarchical work culture, 보고 (the report itself) is a big deal, so you'll often use the humble 보고드리다 when reporting to a superior. The recipient takes 께/에게(한테) and the content takes 을/를. For casually telling a peer something, 말하다 or 알려주다 is more natural; save 보고하다 for official updates.
mistakes: Don't use 보고하다 for chatting with a friend ('telling' them news) — it's specifically an official report; use 말하다/알려주다 instead.

usage: 일단 계획대로 진행할게요.
For now I'll proceed as planned.
진행하다 = to carry a task/process forward; extremely common in project work.
회의는 예정대로 진행됩니다.
The meeting will proceed as scheduled.
진행되다 (passive) = '(something) proceeds/is underway'; pair it with 진행하다.
examples: 이대로 진행해도 될까요?
Is it okay to proceed like this?
Checking with a manager before moving ahead; very polite and common.
지금 어디까지 진행됐어요?
How far along is it now?
Literally 'up to where has it progressed' — standard status check.
다음 단계를 진행하기 전에 한번 확인해 주세요.
Please double-check before we proceed to the next step.
단계 = step/stage; -기 전에 = before doing.
nuance: 진행하다 means to push a task, process, project, or event forward — it's the verb for 'carry out / proceed with' and it's everywhere in Korean office life. The active 진행하다 (you move it forward) pairs with the passive 진행되다 ('it is underway / proceeds'); 진행 상황 means 'status'. It implies an ongoing process with steps, so use it for projects and procedures rather than for finishing a single discrete action.
mistakes: Keep 진행하다 (you carry it out) separate from 진행되다 (it proceeds on its own): 제가 진행할게요 vs. 잘 진행되고 있어요.

usage: 오늘 업무를 다 마쳤어요.
I finished all my work today.
마치다 = to bring something to a proper end; slightly formal, good for work/study.
회의를 마치겠습니다.
Let's conclude the meeting.
마치겠습니다 is the set phrase used to formally wrap up a meeting or event.
examples: 일을 일찍 마치고 집에 갈 거예요.
I'll finish work early and go home.
마치고 = 'having finished, then'; smooth way to link two actions.
이번 분기 보고서를 무사히 마쳤습니다.
I successfully finished this quarter's report.
무사히 = 'safely/without issue', natural with completing a big task.
발표를 마친 뒤에 질문을 받을게요.
I'll take questions after I finish the presentation.
-(으)ㄴ 뒤에 = 'after doing'; common presentation phrasing.
nuance: 마치다 means to finish or conclude something properly — your workday, a meeting, a report, a course. It's transitive (you take an object: 일을 마치다) and carries a slightly formal, 'bringing to a proper close' feeling, which is why announcements use 마치겠습니다. The stem ends in ㅊ + ㅣ, so it conjugates 마쳐요 / 마쳤어요. Compare with the more casual, hands-on 끝내다, and the intransitive 끝나다 ('it ends').
mistakes: 마치다 needs an object (일을 마치다). For 'it ended by itself' use the intransitive 끝나다, not 마치다.

usage: 이것만 끝내고 갈게요.
Let me just finish this and then go.
끝내다 = the everyday 'get it done/wrap it up'; you actively finish something.
오늘 안에 이 일을 끝내야 해요.
I have to get this done by today.
오늘 안에 = 'within today'; 끝내야 해요 expresses a deadline pressure.
examples: 빨리 끝내고 한잔하러 가요.
Let's wrap up quickly and go for a drink.
Casual coworker talk; 한잔하다 = grab a drink after work.
일을 다 못 끝냈어요.
I couldn't finish all the work.
못 + 끝내다 = couldn't manage to finish; 다 = all.
회의를 30분 안에 끝낼 수 있을까요?
Can we wrap up the meeting within 30 minutes?
Practical scheduling question; -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요 = 'do you think we can ~?'
nuance: 끝내다 is the active, everyday verb for finishing or wrapping something up — you make it end. It's the transitive partner of 끝나다 ('it ends on its own'), which is already common: 일을 끝냈어요 (I finished the work) vs. 일이 끝났어요 (the work ended). Compared with 마치다, 끝내다 is more casual and task-focused, perfect for daily office talk like 이것만 끝내고 갈게요. The stem is 끝내- so the past is 끝냈어요.
mistakes: Don't swap 끝내다 (transitive: you finish it) with 끝나다 (intransitive: it finishes): 숙제를 끝냈어요 vs. 수업이 끝났어요.

usage: 계약서를 검토하고 다시 연락드릴게요.
I'll review the contract and get back to you.
검토하다 = to look something over carefully before deciding; very common with documents.
한번 검토해 보고 말씀드릴게요.
I'll take a look and let you know.
검토해 보다 = 'try reviewing it'; softens it to 'let me look into it' before committing.
examples: 이 제안서 좀 검토해 주시겠어요?
Could you review this proposal?
-아/어 주시겠어요 = polite request; standard when asking a colleague to check something.
내부적으로 검토 중입니다.
We're reviewing it internally.
검토 중 = 'under review'; a polite, common way to say 'we're still deciding'.
꼼꼼하게 검토했는데 문제는 없었어요.
I reviewed it carefully and there were no problems.
꼼꼼하게 = thoroughly/meticulously, a valued trait at work.
nuance: 검토하다 means to review or examine something carefully — documents, proposals, plans, contracts — usually before approving or deciding. It's a polished business word, and 검토 중이에요 ('it's under review') is a handy, face-saving way to say a decision hasn't been made yet. It implies careful inspection, not a quick glance, so for casually 'checking' something simple you'd use 확인하다 instead.
mistakes: 검토하다 (carefully examine to decide) is heavier than 확인하다 (just check/confirm) — don't use 검토하다 for quickly confirming a time or fact.

usage: 오늘도 야근해요.
I'm working late again today.
야근하다 = to stay at work past normal hours; 오늘도 ('again today') captures the office mood perfectly.
요즘 야근이 너무 잦아요.
These days I have overtime way too often.
The noun 야근 + 잦다 (frequent) is how people complain about overtime.
examples: 프로젝트 마감 때문에 이번 주 내내 야근했어요.
I worked late all week because of the project deadline.
마감 = deadline; 내내 = the whole time/all through.
야근하지 말고 얼른 들어가세요.
Don't work late, go home soon.
들어가다 here = 'head home'; a caring thing to say to a coworker.
야근하면 저녁은 회사에서 시켜 먹어요.
When I work late, I order dinner at the office.
시켜 먹다 = order food (and eat it); very common overtime reality.
nuance: 야근하다 is the verb every office worker in Korea knows: to stay and work past regular hours. It's neutral in form but usually carries a tired, slightly complaining tone, since overtime is a real part of many workplaces. The noun 야근 appears in lots of phrases (야근 수당 = overtime pay, 야근 자주 해요 = I work late a lot). Note it specifically means working late in the evening; for night-shift schedules you'd say 야간근무.
mistakes: 야근하다 is not generic 'overtime' as a contract concept — that's 초과근무. 야근 specifically = staying and working into the evening.

usage: 저 다음 달에 퇴사해요.
I'm leaving the company next month.
퇴사하다 = to quit/leave your job (resign), the opposite of 입사하다.
회사를 그만두고 싶어서 퇴사하려고요.
I want to quit, so I'm planning to resign.
그만두다 (quit) and 퇴사하다 overlap; 퇴사하다 is the cleaner 'leave the company' term.
examples: 김 대리님 퇴사하셨대요.
I heard Assistant Manager Kim resigned.
-셨대요 = honorific + reported speech ('I heard that ~'); classic office grapevine.
퇴사하기 전에 인수인계를 해야 해요.
Before resigning I have to hand over my work.
인수인계 = handover of duties, a must-do before leaving.
요즘 퇴사하고 싶다는 생각이 자주 들어요.
Lately I often feel like quitting.
-고 싶다는 생각이 들다 = 'the thought of wanting to ~ occurs'; natural way to vent.
nuance: 퇴사하다 means to leave your company — to resign or quit. It's the direct opposite of 입사하다 (to join a company), and the two are a natural pair to learn together. 퇴사 (resignation) is a huge topic among young Korean workers, so you'll hear it constantly along with 이직 (changing jobs) and 인수인계 (handover). Note: 퇴사하다 = leaving the company for good; do not confuse it with 퇴근하다 (going home at the end of a workday).
mistakes: Don't mix up 퇴사하다 (quit the company permanently) with 퇴근하다 (leave the office for the day) — one ends your employment, the other ends your shift.

usage: 작년에 이 회사에 입사했어요.
I joined this company last year.
입사하다 = to enter/join a company as an employee; the company takes 에.
신입으로 입사한 지 6개월 됐어요.
It's been 6 months since I joined as a new hire.
신입 = new recruit; -(으)ㄴ 지 ~ 됐어요 = 'it's been ~ since'.
examples: 언제 입사하셨어요?
When did you join the company?
Friendly question to a coworker; honorific 하셨어요.
원하던 회사에 입사하게 돼서 정말 기뻐요.
I'm so happy I got to join the company I wanted.
원하던 = 'that I had wanted'; -게 돼서 = 'because it turned out that'.
입사한 첫날이라 아직 아무것도 몰라요.
It's my first day at the company, so I don't know anything yet.
첫날 = first day; common new-employee line.
nuance: 입사하다 means to join a company as an employee — your starting point, the mirror image of 퇴사하다 (to leave). The company you join takes the particle 에 (이 회사에 입사하다). It pairs with terms new workers hear daily: 신입 (new hire), 입사 동기 (people who joined the same year), 입사 지원 (job application). Learn 입사하다 / 퇴사하다 as a set so you can talk clearly about starting and leaving jobs.
mistakes: The company takes 에, not 을/를: 회사에 입사했어요, not 회사를 입사했어요.

usage: 오후에 팀이랑 회의해요.
I have a meeting with my team this afternoon.
회의하다 = to hold/have a meeting; the people you meet with take (이)랑/와/과.
이 건은 회의해서 정하기로 해요.
Let's decide this matter by discussing it in a meeting.
회의해서 = 'by meeting/discussing then'; natural for deciding things together.
examples: 지금 회의 중이라 나중에 전화할게요.
I'm in a meeting right now, so I'll call later.
회의 중 (the noun + 중) = 'in a meeting'; you'll text this constantly.
내일 10시에 회의하기로 했어요.
We agreed to meet at 10 tomorrow.
-기로 했어요 = 'we decided/agreed to'; standard for setting a meeting.
다 같이 모여서 한번 회의해 봅시다.
Let's all get together and have a meeting.
-아/어 봅시다 = 'let's try ~'; -ㅂ시다 is a confident formal suggestion to the team.
nuance: 회의하다 means to hold or have a meeting — the daily reality of office life. In practice the noun 회의 shows up even more: 회의 중이에요 (I'm in a meeting), 회의 잡다 (set up a meeting), 회의실 (meeting room). The people you meet with take (이)랑/와/과. For a quick informal chat you might say 잠깐 얘기하다 instead, but for a scheduled, purposeful discussion 회의하다 is exactly right.
mistakes: For a casual quick chat, use 얘기하다/이야기하다 — 회의하다 implies a real, scheduled meeting, not a two-minute hallway talk.
